function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the whole workflow.  
I’ve also included the exact contents of the files that will be created/updated.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually run `git clone`, `git push`, etc. from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the repo (optional – just to confirm)

```bash
# Install the helper script (if you want to run the analysis yourself)
# (The helper is a tiny Python script that counts lines per language.)
# For the purpose of this guide we’ll skip the actual analysis and assume it’s a pure Node.js repo.
```

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile for nodejs-welcome
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set maintainer (optional)
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is a small, production‑ready image.  
> * `npm ci --only=production` installs only the production dependencies.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** (common for Node.js).  
>   If your app uses a different port, change the `EXPOSE` line accordingly.

### 2.3 Create Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and add a file `deployment.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- adjust if you use a different registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **Notes**  
> * `replicas: 3` – you can change this to whatever you need.  
> * `image:` – if you’re pushing to Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, or another registry, update the image name accordingly.  
> * `type: ClusterIP` – exposes the service only inside the cluster. Use `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions workflow

Create a directory `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker tag zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to set up**  
> * Create two GitHub secrets in the repo settings:  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password).  
> * If you’re using GitHub Container Registry, replace the login step with `docker/login-action@v3` using `registry: ghcr.io` and the appropriate secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you want to add everything that was changed (including any other new files), you can simply run `git add .`.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run on the `main` branch, build the Docker image, and push it to Docker Hub.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .

# Verify Kubernetes manifests apply (requires a cluster)
kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

If everything builds and applies without errors, you’re good to go!

---

### Recap of what was created

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes Docker image |

Feel free to tweak the values (image names, ports, replica counts, etc.) to match your exact environment. Happy coding!
